source.title: Basic Inequalities for First-Order Optimization with Applications to Statistical Risk Analysis
source.authors: Seung-Jin Paik; Kang-Jie Zhou; Matus Telgarsky; R. Tibshirani

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports prediction-risk curves along optimization trajectories, which bear on the time-wise risk-shape version, but studies GLM optimization rather than deep-network double descent.
record.gate_note: The paper does not sweep model size or training-sample size. It does report prediction risk against total elapsed optimization time and characterizes the selected curves as U-shaped; only these time-path results are recorded. Its comparisons of implicit and explicit regularization are not separate evidence about double descent.
record.test_reason: The paper is a convex-optimization and statistics study. It derives basic inequalities linking early-stopped GD/EGD to ridge/KL regularization in GLMs, plus excess-risk bounds. It never mentions or cites double descent. Its risk-vs-elapsed-time curves (Fig. 2) come from linear, logistic and Poisson GLMs, not deep networks. The SNR parameter γ was chosen on purpose to make the curves 'U-shaped', so the curve shape is a design selection, not an outcome. None of this bears on whether epoch-wise or model-wise double descent occurs. 'cites_only' is the closest enum value; the paper does not actually cite the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is theoretical. Basic inequalities give a unified framework linking implicit and explicit regularization. They yield early-stopping excess-risk bounds matching ridge (Õ(√(d/n))) and KL (Õ(√(log d/n))) rates. Experiments show close alignment of training dynamics, risk curves and solution paths, with neither approach dominating minimum risk. Double descent is never addressed.
record.recipe_differences: Studies first-order optimization and prediction risk in GLMs; it does not reproduce the original model-size, epoch-wise double-descent, or sample-size interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The experiments choose γ values to obtain U-shaped rather than uninterestingly monotonic risk curves; the tasks, regimes, and γ values vary.

fits_no_version.finding: In convex GLMs (linear, logistic, Poisson), early-stopped GD/EGD risk over elapsed time closely tracks explicit ridge/KL risk over 1/λ. The curves are single U-shapes at the chosen γ, and neither approach dominates in minimum risk.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early stopping in convex GLMs acts like explicit ridge/KL regularization, giving classical U-shaped time-wise risk.

record.problems: The evidence relevant to V2 is qualitative and conveyed through curve descriptions/plots, with no reported uncertainty for these curves. The experiments use synthetic GLM tasks rather than deep networks and vary elapsed time rather than epochs.
record.rows_left_out: No results relevant to the other claim versions were reported. Explicit-regularization curves are excluded because they vary regularization rather than training time.

untested.parts: No deep networks. Time curves were selected to be U-shaped, with no search for a second descent.
No noise-driven peak or multiple-descent analysis. The regularization comparisons are not about removing a peak.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' and its V2 limits_scope label should be dropped. The U-shaped curves are an artifact of γ selection (the paper says γ was chosen to avoid monotonic risk), in convex models outside V2's scope. The record's 'absent' states are also wrong: the curves cannot show presence or absence of a second descent.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
Tests elapsed optimization time in GLM estimator tasks, not deep-network epoch counts or the original deep-network setting.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes or interpolation-point analysis.
No unified effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
No analysis of noise-driven peaks, multiple descent peaks, or optimally tuned regularization eliminating such peaks.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number or analysis of a resulting curve.
